points: Soil cadmium concentration fell from 4.8 mg per kg to 2.1 mg per kg over 112 days, a reduction of 56 percent on a dry mass basis.
Shoot cadmium concentration reached 18.6 mg per kg dry mass, and root cadmium concentration reached 31.4 mg per kg dry mass.
The translocation factor was 0.59 for cadmium in the tested cultivar.
Shoot dry biomass was 6.2 tonnes per hectare, and total cadmium uptake in the shoots was 115 g per hectare.
Soil zinc concentration fell from 148 mg per kg to 130 mg per kg, a reduction of 12 percent.
Soil pH (pH: the negative logarithm of hydrogen ion activity) was 6.4 at planting and at harvest.
definitions: phytoremediation = the use of plants to remove or immobilise contaminants in soil
translocation factor = the ratio of shoot metal concentration to root metal concentration
dry mass basis = concentrations expressed per unit mass of material dried to constant mass
limits: Results come from one field site and one growing season, and the uptake values apply to the tested cultivar at the stated soil pH.
prose: Phytoremediation (the use of plants to remove or immobilise contaminants in soil) reduced the cadmium concentration of the field soil during one growing season. Soil cadmium concentration fell from 4.8 mg per kg to 2.1 mg per kg over 112 days, a reduction of 56 percent on a dry mass basis (dry mass basis: concentrations expressed per unit mass of material dried to constant mass). The reduction was recorded in every replicate plot, and the plot means carried the same direction of change at each sampling date. Shoot cadmium concentration reached 18.6 mg per kg dry mass, and root cadmium concentration reached 31.4 mg per kg dry mass. Root tissue held the larger share of the accumulated cadmium, and shoot tissue held the smaller share. The translocation factor (the ratio of shoot metal concentration to root metal concentration) was 0.59 for cadmium in the tested cultivar. A translocation factor below one marks a plant that retains metal in the roots, and retention in the roots limits the mass removed at harvest. Shoot dry biomass was 6.2 tonnes per hectare, and total cadmium uptake in the shoots was 115 g per hectare. Harvest of the shoots removes that cadmium mass from the field, and regrowth in a second season would be required for further removal. Soil zinc concentration fell from 148 mg per kg to 130 mg per kg, a reduction of 12 percent. The zinc reduction was smaller than the cadmium reduction, and zinc uptake competed with cadmium uptake in the same root tissue. Soil pH (the negative logarithm of hydrogen ion activity) was 6.4 at planting and at harvest, and pH drift does not account for the change in soil cadmium concentration. Results come from one field site and one growing season, and the uptake values apply to the tested cultivar at the stated soil pH. Application to other soils requires a site trial, because soil texture and soil organic matter change root uptake.

points: The reversible cell voltage was 1.23 V at the test temperature of 80 degrees C and a reactant pressure of 150 kPa.
Open-circuit voltage was 0.96 V for the tested membrane electrode assembly.
Cell voltage at a current density of 0.8 A per square centimetre was 0.68 V.
Losses at that current density were activation loss 0.13 V, ohmic loss 0.09 V, and concentration loss 0.06 V, summing to 0.28 V against the open-circuit voltage.
Area-specific resistance was 0.11 ohm square centimetres, consistent with the ohmic loss at the stated current density.
At a current density of 1.6 A per square centimetre, cell voltage was 0.52 V and concentration loss dominated the added loss.
Voltage efficiency at the 0.8 A per square centimetre point was 55 percent relative to the reversible voltage.
definitions: proton exchange membrane fuel cell = a fuel cell in which a polymer membrane conducts protons from anode to cathode
activation loss = the voltage loss from the finite rate of the electrode reactions
ohmic loss = the voltage loss from ionic and electronic resistance in the cell
concentration loss = the voltage loss from depletion of reactants at the electrode surface
area-specific resistance = cell resistance multiplied by active area
limits: Loss values apply to the tested membrane electrode assembly at the stated temperature and pressure, with humidified reactants.
prose: Voltage losses in the proton exchange membrane fuel cell (a fuel cell in which a polymer membrane conducts protons from anode to cathode) were measured against the reversible voltage at each current density. The reversible cell voltage was 1.23 V at the test temperature of 80 degrees C and a reactant pressure of 150 kPa. Open-circuit voltage was 0.96 V for the tested membrane electrode assembly, and the gap between open-circuit voltage and reversible voltage records crossover and internal currents at zero load. Cell voltage at a current density of 0.8 A per square centimetre was 0.68 V. Losses at that current density were activation loss 0.13 V, ohmic loss 0.09 V, and concentration loss 0.06 V, summing to 0.28 V against the open-circuit voltage. Activation loss (the voltage loss from the finite rate of the electrode reactions) was the largest single component at this operating point. Ohmic loss (the voltage loss from ionic and electronic resistance in the cell) grew in proportion to current density across the measured range. Concentration loss (the voltage loss from depletion of reactants at the electrode surface) remained the smallest component at moderate current density. Area-specific resistance (cell resistance multiplied by active area) was 0.11 ohm square centimetres, consistent with the ohmic loss at the stated current density. At a current density of 1.6 A per square centimetre, cell voltage was 0.52 V and concentration loss dominated the added loss. The polarisation curve bent downward in that region, and reactant supply at the cathode limited the current. Voltage efficiency at the 0.8 A per square centimetre point was 55 percent relative to the reversible voltage. Loss values apply to the tested membrane electrode assembly at the stated temperature and pressure, with humidified reactants, and a drier feed raises the ohmic component.

points: Feed solute concentration was 12.4 g per litre and raffinate solute concentration was 3.1 g per litre at a solvent to feed mass ratio of 1.5 and a temperature of 25 degrees C.
Solute removal was 75 percent of the feed solute, and solute removed per litre of feed was 9.3 g per litre.
Mean Murphree stage efficiency was 68 percent, with stage values from 62 percent to 71 percent across the column.
Efficiency fell at the feed stage, where the entering feed raised local loading, and efficiency held steady at the solvent entry stage.
definitions: liquid-liquid extraction = separation of a solute between two immiscible liquid phases
raffinate = the feed phase after contact with the solvent
extract = the solvent phase after contact with the feed
Murphree stage efficiency = the actual composition change across a stage divided by the composition change at equilibrium, expressed as a percentage
limits: Efficiency values apply to the tested solute and solvent pair at the stated temperature and phase ratio.
prose: Stage efficiency in the liquid-liquid extraction column (liquid-liquid extraction: separation of a solute between two immiscible liquid phases) was measured stage by stage at steady state. Feed solute concentration was 12.4 g per litre and raffinate solute concentration was 3.1 g per litre at a solvent to feed mass ratio of 1.5 and a temperature of 25 degrees C. The raffinate (the feed phase after contact with the solvent) left the column at the feed end, and the extract (the solvent phase after contact with the feed) left at the solvent entry end. Solute removal was 75 percent of the feed solute, and solute removed per litre of feed was 9.3 g per litre. Removal at this level met the separation target for the downstream step, and the raffinate passed to solvent recovery without a second extraction pass. Mean Murphree stage efficiency (the actual composition change across a stage divided by the composition change at equilibrium, expressed as a percentage) was 68 percent, with stage values from 62 percent to 71 percent across the column. Efficiency fell at the feed stage, where the entering feed raised local loading, and efficiency held steady at the solvent entry stage. The feed stage carried the highest solute flux in the column, and droplet size at the feed stage was larger than droplet size at the lean stages. Larger droplets present less interfacial area per unit volume, and the measured efficiency follows the interfacial area. Stage efficiency in the middle of the column varied little between sampling rounds, and steady state is a fair description of the middle stages. Efficiency values apply to the tested solute and solvent pair at the stated temperature and phase ratio, and a change of solvent changes both the equilibrium and the efficiency.

points: Initial sugar concentration was 108 g per litre and final sugar concentration was 9 g per litre after 96 hours at 18 degrees C, an attenuation of 92 percent.
Ethanol concentration at the end of fermentation was 5.1 percent by volume.
Peak specific growth rate of the yeast was 0.21 per hour, and the lag phase lasted 8 hours after pitching.
Yeast concentration rose from a pitch concentration of 0.6 g per litre to a final concentration of 1.8 g per litre on a dry mass basis.
Final pH was 4.2 for the fermented beer.
Final diacetyl concentration was 0.08 mg per litre, below the flavour threshold of 0.10 mg per litre used in the brewery laboratory.
definitions: specific growth rate = the rate of yeast mass increase per unit yeast mass
lag phase = the period after pitching in which measurable yeast growth has not begun
attenuation = the fraction of the original sugar consumed during fermentation, expressed as a percentage
pitching = the addition of yeast to wort at the start of fermentation
diacetyl = a fermentation by-product with a butter-like flavour at concentrations above its threshold
limits: Kinetic values apply to the tested yeast strain, wort composition and fermentation temperature.
prose: Fermentation kinetics for the tested yeast strain were recorded from pitching (the addition of yeast to wort at the start of fermentation) to the final gravity reading. Initial sugar concentration was 108 g per litre and final sugar concentration was 9 g per litre after 96 hours at 18 degrees C, an attenuation of 92 percent (attenuation: the fraction of the original sugar consumed during fermentation, expressed as a percentage). Sugar consumption was fastest during the middle of the fermentation, and the consumption rate fell as the sugar concentration fell. Ethanol concentration at the end of fermentation was 5.1 percent by volume. Ethanol accumulated in step with sugar consumption, and ethanol accumulation slowed yeast growth late in the fermentation. Peak specific growth rate (the rate of yeast mass increase per unit yeast mass) of the yeast was 0.21 per hour, and the lag phase (the period after pitching in which measurable yeast growth has not begun) lasted 8 hours after pitching. The lag phase length matches the pitching rate and the wort oxygen content of this brew, and a shorter lag phase follows a higher pitching rate. Yeast concentration rose from a pitch concentration of 0.6 g per litre to a final concentration of 1.8 g per litre on a dry mass basis. Final pH (pH: the negative logarithm of hydrogen ion activity) was 4.2 for the fermented beer. The pH fell during active growth and held steady after sugar exhaustion. Final diacetyl concentration was 0.08 mg per litre, below the flavour threshold of 0.10 mg per litre used in the brewery laboratory. Diacetyl (a fermentation by-product with a butter-like flavour at concentrations above its threshold) peaked during active growth and fell during the rest period at the end of fermentation. Kinetic values apply to the tested yeast strain, wort composition and fermentation temperature.

points: Take a basis of 100 kg per hour of fresh feed of reactant A.
Single-pass conversion in the reactor is 50 percent of the reactant entering the reactor.
The separator returns unreacted reactant as the recycle stream, and a purge stream removes 10 percent of the unreacted reactant leaving the separator.
The unreacted reactant leaving the separator is 91 kg per hour, split into a recycle stream of 82 kg per hour and a purge stream of 9 kg per hour.
Overall conversion is 91 percent of the fresh feed.
definitions: material balance = an accounting of the mass entering, leaving, reacting and accumulating in a system
recycle stream = a stream returned from a downstream unit to an upstream unit
purge stream = a stream withdrawn from a recycle loop to prevent accumulation
single-pass conversion = the fraction of a reactant converted during one passage through the reactor
overall conversion = the fraction of the fresh feed of a reactant converted in the whole process
limits: The worked example treats the separator as perfect and the reaction as the only mass change in the loop.
prose: This tutorial works a material balance (an accounting of the mass entering, leaving, reacting and accumulating in a system) for a reactor with a recycle stream (a stream returned from a downstream unit to an upstream unit). The result at the end is the overall conversion of the loop, and each step can be checked against the step before it. Take a basis of 100 kg per hour of fresh feed of reactant A. Write the reactor inlet as the fresh feed plus the recycle stream, and keep the recycle flow as an unknown until the separator balance fixes the recycle flow. Single-pass conversion (the fraction of a reactant converted during one passage through the reactor) in the reactor is 50 percent of the reactant entering the reactor. The separator returns unreacted reactant as the recycle stream, and a purge stream (a stream withdrawn from a recycle loop to prevent accumulation) removes 10 percent of the unreacted reactant leaving the separator. Write the separator balance next. The unreacted reactant leaving the separator is 91 kg per hour, split into a recycle stream of 82 kg per hour and a purge stream of 9 kg per hour. Check the split at this point: the recycle stream and the purge stream sum to the unreacted flow, and the purge stream is the stated fraction of that flow. The reactor inlet is the fresh feed plus the recycle stream, and half of the inlet reacts in one pass. The unreacted half matches the flow leaving the separator, and the balance closes. Overall conversion (the fraction of the fresh feed of a reactant converted in the whole process) is 91 percent of the fresh feed. The gap between single-pass conversion and overall conversion is the recycle stream at work: unreacted reactant returns to the reactor and reacts on a later pass, and only the purge stream carries reactant out of the loop unreacted. The worked example treats the separator as perfect and the reaction as the only mass change in the loop.

points: The Antoine equation gives the base-10 logarithm of the vapour pressure P (P: vapour pressure, in mmHg) as A minus B divided by the sum of T and C, with T the temperature in degrees C and A, B and C substance constants.
For water, A is 8.07131, B is 1730.63 and C is 233.426, with P in mmHg and T in degrees C.
At T equal to 50 degrees C, the sum of T and C is 283.426 degrees C and the quotient B over that sum is 6.106.
The base-10 logarithm of P is 8.07131 minus 6.106, which is 1.965.
Raising 10 to the power 1.965 gives P equal to 92.3 mmHg.
Conversion at 101.325 kPa per 760 mmHg gives a vapour pressure of 12.3 kPa.
definitions: vapour pressure = the pressure exerted by a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid at a stated temperature
Antoine equation = an empirical relation between vapour pressure and temperature with three substance constants
mmHg = a pressure unit, the pressure of a mercury column one millimetre high
limits: The constants hold between 1 degree C and 100 degrees C, and the calculation inherits that range.
prose: This tutorial calculates a vapour pressure (the pressure exerted by a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid at a stated temperature) from the Antoine equation (an empirical relation between vapour pressure and temperature with three substance constants). The outcome is the vapour pressure of water at the stated temperature, in mmHg (a pressure unit, the pressure of a mercury column one millimetre high) and in kilopascals. The Antoine equation gives the base-10 logarithm of the vapour pressure P as A minus B divided by the sum of T and C, with T the temperature in degrees C and A, B and C substance constants. The symbols stand in symbol order: P is the vapour pressure, T is the temperature, and A, B and C are the constants for the substance and the temperature range. For water, A is 8.07131, B is 1730.63 and C is 233.426, with P in mmHg and T in degrees C. At T equal to 50 degrees C, the sum of T and C is 283.426 degrees C and the quotient B over that sum is 6.106. The base-10 logarithm of P is 8.07131 minus 6.106, which is 1.965. Raising 10 to the power 1.965 gives P equal to 92.3 mmHg. Check the result at this point against the trend of the property: vapour pressure rises with temperature, and the calculated value sits between the values at the neighbouring round temperatures in a standard table. Conversion at 101.325 kPa per 760 mmHg gives a vapour pressure of 12.3 kPa. Keep the pressure unit attached to the constant set throughout a calculation, because a constant set fitted in mmHg returns a pressure in mmHg. The constants hold between 1 degree C and 100 degrees C, and the calculation inherits that range. A temperature outside the range needs a constant set fitted over that range.

points: The particle diameter d is 80 micrometres, the particle density is 2600 kg per cubic metre, and the fluid density is 1000 kg per cubic metre, giving a density difference of 1600 kg per cubic metre.
The fluid viscosity is 0.001 pascal seconds and the acceleration due to gravity g is 9.81 metres per second per second.
Stokes law gives the terminal velocity v as g times d squared times the density difference, divided by 18 times the viscosity.
Substitution gives v equal to 0.0056 metres per second, which is 5.6 millimetres per second.
The particle Reynolds number at the calculated velocity is 0.45, below the Stokes regime limit of 1.
definitions: terminal velocity = the settling velocity at which drag on a particle balances the particle weight minus buoyancy
Stokes law = the drag relation for a sphere at low Reynolds number, and the settling relation derived from that drag relation
Reynolds number = the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces in a flow
sedimentation = the settling of suspended particles under gravity
limits: Stokes law holds for spherical particles in the stated Reynolds number range, in a dilute suspension with no wall effects.
prose: This tutorial calculates the terminal velocity (the settling velocity at which drag on a particle balances the particle weight minus buoyancy) of a single particle settling by sedimentation (the settling of suspended particles under gravity). The outcome is the settling velocity in metres per second, with a regime check at the end. The particle diameter d is 80 micrometres, the particle density is 2600 kg per cubic metre, and the fluid density is 1000 kg per cubic metre, giving a density difference of 1600 kg per cubic metre. The fluid viscosity is 0.001 pascal seconds and the acceleration due to gravity g is 9.81 metres per second per second. Stokes law (the drag relation for a sphere at low Reynolds number, and the settling relation derived from that drag relation) gives the terminal velocity v as g times d squared times the density difference, divided by 18 times the viscosity. The symbols stand in the order of the relation: v is the terminal velocity, g is the acceleration due to gravity, d is the particle diameter, the two densities are the particle density and the fluid density, and the viscosity closes the relation. Substitution gives v equal to 0.0056 metres per second, which is 5.6 millimetres per second. Check the units at this point: the relation returns a length divided by a time, and the millimetre form suits a settling column reading. The particle Reynolds number (the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces in a flow) at the calculated velocity is 0.45, below the Stokes regime limit of 1. A Reynolds number in this range keeps the drag relation valid, and a value near or past the limit needs a drag correlation for the transitional regime. Stokes law holds for spherical particles in the stated Reynolds number range, in a dilute suspension with no wall effects.

points: The study prepares a porous carbon electrode material for a supercapacitor and measures the electrode in an aqueous electrolyte.
Specific capacitance of the material was 248 farads per gram at an electrode loading of 2.0 mg per square centimetre.
The measured surface area of the carbon was 1420 square metres per gram.
Energy density of the device was 34.4 watt hours per kilogram across a voltage window of 1.0 V.
Power density of the device was 8.5 kilowatts per kilogram.
Capacitance retention was 94 percent after 10000 charge and discharge cycles.
definitions: supercapacitor = an electrochemical device that stores charge at an electrode and electrolyte interface
specific capacitance = capacitance per unit mass of active electrode material
capacitance retention = the fraction of the initial capacitance retained after cycling, expressed as a percentage
prose: Charge storage in a supercapacitor (an electrochemical device that stores charge at an electrode and electrolyte interface) depends on the accessible surface of the electrode material, and carbon electrodes trade surface area against electrical conductivity. This study prepares a porous carbon electrode material and measures the electrode in an aqueous electrolyte against that trade. The carbon was formed by carbonisation of a polymer precursor and activation in steam, and the electrode was tested in a two-electrode cell. Specific capacitance (capacitance per unit mass of active electrode material) of the material was 248 farads per gram at an electrode loading of 2.0 mg per square centimetre. The measured surface area of the carbon was 1420 square metres per gram, and the capacitance tracks the surface area across the sample set. Energy density of the device was 34.4 watt hours per kilogram across a voltage window of 1.0 V. Power density of the device was 8.5 kilowatts per kilogram. Capacitance retention (the fraction of the initial capacitance retained after cycling, expressed as a percentage) was 94 percent after 10000 charge and discharge cycles. The retention records a pore structure that survives repeated cycling, and the material suits applications that cycle the device many times over a service life.
